title: Biological legacies influence seedling survival and growth in post‐fire restoration of Patagonian Nothofagus pumilio forests
content:
In post-fire subantarctic forests of Torres del Paine National Park, nucleation-based reforestation of Nothofagus pumilio was evaluated over 5 years to assess how the identity, proximity, and lateral coverage of biological legacies influence seedling survival and growth. Using microsite-scale measurements and linear mixed-effects models, we found that proximity to shrubs and fallen logs significantly increased survival and growth, particularly within 1.5–3.5 m and under lateral coverage ≥40%. These findings provide operational guidelines for optimizing planting nuclei placement in post-fire, non-resprouting forest restoration.


Abstract

High-severity wildfires increasingly affect the subantarctic forests of southern Patagonia, where fires have left extensive areas with limited natural regeneration in forests dominated by Nothofagus pumilio (lenga). In Torres del Paine National Park, repeated large fires have created degraded landscapes in which seedling establishment is constrained by harsh microclimatic conditions. Since 2012, nucleation-based reforestation has been implemented across more than 470 ha using planting clusters associated with biological legacies such as shrubs, fallen logs, and standing dead trees. Although these structures are assumed to function as nurse elements, their spatial configuration and relative influence on seedling performance remain poorly quantified. We evaluated how legacy identity, proximity, and lateral coverage influence N. pumilio seedling survival and growth 2 and 5 years after planting. Using microsite-scale measurements and linear mixed-effects models, we assessed the effects of legacy structure on survival, maximum height, and cumulative growth. Proximity to shrubs and fallen logs significantly increased survival and growth, particularly within distances of approximately 1.5–3.5 m and under moderate to high lateral coverage. Nuclei dominated by a single substantial legacy performed better than those surrounded by dispersed or structurally mixed elements. Practical implication: Microsite configuration is a key determinant of restoration success. Practitioners can enhance seedling survival and growth in post-fire subantarctic forests by positioning planting nuclei approximately 1.5–3.5 m from large shrubs or fallen logs, prioritizing microsites dominated by a single structurally substantial legacy over spatially dispersed configuration.

Resumen

Los incendios de alta severidad afectan cada vez más los bosques subantárticos del sur de Patagonia, dejando extensas áreas con regeneración natural escasa en bosques dominados por Nothofagus pumilio (lenga). En el Parque Nacional Torres del Paine, incendios recurrentes han degradado el paisaje al punto en que el establecimiento de plántulas queda limitado por condiciones micro climáticas extremas. Desde 2012 se ha implementado reforestación en núcleos en más de 470 ha, ubicando grupos de plantación junto a legados biológicos como arbustos, troncos caídos y árboles muertos en pie. Sin embargo, la configuración espacial de estas estructuras y su influencia real sobre el desempeño de las plántulas permanecen insuficientemente evaluadas. Evaluamos cómo la identidad, la proximidad y la cobertura lateral de los legados biológicos afectan la supervivencia y el crecimiento de plántulas de N. pumilio a los dos y cinco años de plantación, mediante mediciones a escala de micrositio y modelos lineales mixtos. La proximidad a arbustos y troncos caídos aumentó significativamente la supervivencia y el crecimiento, especialmente entre 1.5 y 3.5 m de distancia y bajo coberturas laterales moderadas a altas. Los núcleos dominados por un único legado estructuralmente prominente superaron en desempeño a aquellos rodeados por elementos dispersos o mixtos. Implicancia práctica: La configuración espacial del micrositio es un factor determinante del éxito de la restauración. Para mejorar la supervivencia y el crecimiento de plántulas en bosques subantárticos post-fuego, se recomienda posicionar los núcleos de plantación a 1.5–3.5 m de arbustos o troncos caídos de gran tamaño, priorizando micrositios donde un único legado estructuralmente prominente domina el entorno.
